title: There's a $12,000 Reason to Consider Investing in QQQ Over SPY, but It Comes With a Caveat

Credit: Getty Images

The past two decades have been dominated by digital innovations. From mobile to social to cloud computing and now AI, technology and communication services companies have become the biggest stocks on the planet.

The Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) exchange-traded fund, which comprises the 100 largest nonfinancial stocks on the Nasdaq, has been a great way to play the market's biggest secular growth story of the past 20 years. Just look at this murderers' row of its five biggest holdings: Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Micron Technology (MU) and Amazon.com (AMZN), which collectively account for 30% of the ETF.

When it comes to cheap and easy diversification, you can't go wrong with an S&P 500 ETF, such as the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO) or SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY).

Technology and communications names account for almost 48% of the S&P 500, but holding five times the number of stocks versus QQQ means the mega-caps have less influence. Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia represent a significantly larger percentage of QQQ's total assets, amplifying its returns as those specific companies have reached multi-trillion-dollar valuations.

The S&P 500 also holds lots of banking and insurance stocks, which, as noted above, QQQ excludes. The great financial crisis and subsequent era of rock-bottom interest rates did the financial sector — and the S&P 500 — few favors. Financial stocks account for almost 12% of the benchmark index today.

Track all markets on TradingView

The steady ascent of tech and the worst downturn since the 1930s pretty much explain QQQ's extraordinary returns over the past 20 years. To be sure, the S&P 500 has been very good to patient investors, but it lags QQQ by wide margins.

The bottom line on QQQ vs SPY
Credit: YCharts

Have a look at the above chart and you'll see that if you invested $1,000 in QQQ 20 years ago, it would today be worth $20,000. That's good for an annualized total return (price change plus reinvested dividends) of 16.1%.

By comparison, the same sum socked away in SPY would be worth $8,000, or 11% annualized. That's pretty darn good and, importantly, it came with much less volatility.

This last point is key. As they say on Wall Street, there is no such thing as a free lunch. True, QQQ greatly outperformed the broader market, but that outperformance is a risk premium. When the Federal Reserve started rapidly raising interest rates in 2021 and 2022, QQQ fell 36% from its peak. SPY suffered a drawdown of roughly 25%.

Anthropic has released its S-1 registration document, which highlights how its business runs and gives investors a chance to understand the company before it goes public. It's slated to be the biggest IPO ever, likely debuting with a market cap of around $2 trillion. While Anthropic may be the featured company in its own S-1, there are several other stocks that could thrive based on the information in this document.

The five that I think have the most to gain are Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO), Taiwan Semiconductor (NYSE: TSM), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL). There are two primary categories here, but each of them is an investable theme.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Computing suppliers have a bullish outlook based on Anthropic's information

Two of the most notable points in Anthropic's S-1 are just how much money the AI lab has spent on compute already, and how much it plans to spend. Over the next decade, it plans to spend around $518 billion on computing infrastructure. That's a massive amount of money, but Anthropic isn't hosting all of the workloads that utilize its platform.

While the average Claude user may use the webpage or app to work, most businesses will choose to host their Claude instances on their own servers to keep the information that they enter into the platform sequestered. That requires those companies to run the workloads on servers they lease from external cloud providers, which means a substantially greater amount of infrastructure will be needed beyond the $518 billion worth that Anthropic's planning for.

As two of Anthropic's primary computing unit providers, Nvidia and Broadcom should thrive over the next decade as more AI computing power is built out to handle those growing workloads. Taiwan Semiconductor will also be a beneficiary because it manufactures the chips designed by both Nvidia and Broadcom. These three stocks are the cornerstones of my personal AI computing power basket, and each looks like a tremendous buy right now.

AVGO PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts.

All trade for less than 20 times next year's expected earnings, which makes them great values, as Anthropic has confirmed that the AI data center build-out will last for many more years.

(Bloomberg) -- The stock market got a long-awaited jolt of volatility late last week after disappointing earnings from technology giants added to angst around the AI-driven rally.

Now traders are bracing for further shocks this week from the US midterm elections and Nvidia Corp. earnings later in November.

The Cboe Volatility Index on Friday touched the highest intraday level since April as the S&P 500 dropped the most since June. The premium for puts protecting against further losses also surged, as did correlations among stocks, which can signal broader stress in the market. Still, those measures remain well below the levels in March after the US and Israel attacked Iran.

With Nvidia due to report earnings, following disappointing results from Amazon.com Inc., Alphabet Inc. and Intel Corp., investors are preparing for more episodes of volatility. Traders are also eyeing US midterm election results for the potential effect on the war in Iran and domestic economic policy.

"This looks more like a bullish rotation with a derating at its core than the beginning of a broad market deterioration.," said Florian Ielpo, head of macro research at Lombard Odier Investment Management.

So far, the latest selloff has been largely focused on the technology sector, with investors rotating away from the high-flying firms that led the gains this year. Realized 60-day volatility on the US benchmark last week touched the lowest in more than a year, with the low correlation this year and tendency of zero-day options traders to buy dips and sell rallies helping to restrain moves.

The late-week slide comes in a year that's been relatively placid. While 2025 saw a cluster of extreme market swings around the tariff tumult in April, in 2026 US stocks have largely shrugged off spikes in oil prices and interest rates.

But even as the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 capped its worst month since 2025, some investors were betting on a recovery. There were pockets of call and call spread buying seen Friday on the benchmark indexes and some of the most beaten-down tech names such as Intel.

Options were relatively pricey before the larger gyrations late in the week, with the VIX at the higher end of the range over the past five years compared with 20-day realized swings.

title: AMZN Q3 deep dive: cloud surge and AI investments drive mixed market reception

AMZN Q3 deep dive: cloud surge and AI investments drive mixed market reception

Cloud computing and online retail behemoth Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) met Wall Street's revenue expectations in Q3 2026, with sales up 12.1% year on year to $201.9 billion. The company expects next quarter's revenue to be around $243.5 billion, close to analysts' estimates. Its non-GAAP profit of $1.89 per share was 3.4% below analysts' consensus estimates.

Is now the time to buy AMZN? Find out in our full research report (it's free).

Amazon (AMZN) Q3 2026 highlights:

Revenue $201.9 billion vs S&P analysts' estimates of $202.3 billion (in line)

EPS (GAAP) $1.89 vs analyst expectations of $1.96 (3.4% miss)

Operating margin 13.9%, up from 9.7% in the same quarter last year

Market capitalization $2.63 trillion

StockStory's take

Amazon's third quarter results were shaped by rapid expansion in its cloud business and ongoing momentum in online retail, but a lower-than-expected profit weighed on investor sentiment. Management emphasized that Amazon Web Services (AWS) posted its fastest growth in nearly five years, powered by demand for AI-related infrastructure and a broad set of new customer use cases. CEO Andy Jassy highlighted that AWS "grew 39.3% year-over-year, accelerating for the sixth straight quarter," and continued investment in custom chips and fulfillment efficiencies helped offset higher transportation costs. However, the company's GAAP earnings per share came in below Wall Street forecasts, prompting a significant negative market reaction.

Looking forward, Amazon's guidance is anchored by expectations of continued strength in both AWS and its core retail operations, underpinned by major investments in AI, robotics, and fulfillment. Management pointed to a sizeable AWS backlog and growing customer adoption of new AI services, with Jassy stating, "We believe that AWS can grow north of 40% in each of 2027 and in 2028 and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years." CFO Brian Olsavsky noted that ongoing capital expenditures, particularly in AI and cloud, are expected to drive long-term revenue and free cash flow, though near-term profitability may fluctuate due to higher operating costs and the timing of new product launches.

Key insights from management's remarks

Amazon's management attributed Q3 performance to accelerating cloud growth, strong retail execution, and disciplined investment in AI and fulfillment infrastructure.

AWS growth acceleration: AWS revenue growth accelerated for the sixth consecutive quarter, with management crediting strong demand for both core cloud and AI services. Jassy noted that AWS backlog grew in the triple digits year-over-year, and new AI products like Bedrock and custom chips such as Trainium and Graviton are driving customer adoption and cost efficiencies.

AI and custom silicon momentum: The company's investments in custom silicon, particularly Trainium and Graviton chips, are yielding performance and price advantages for AWS customers. Management said customers using custom silicon saved more than $2 billion in Q3 alone, and revenue commitments for these chips increased over 20 times year-over-year.

Retail and fulfillment leverage: Amazon's core retail segments benefited from fulfillment improvements and increased delivery speeds, with management citing a fourth consecutive year of lowering cost to serve per unit. The expansion of same-day and ultrafast delivery, along with greater use of robotics in fulfillment centers, was highlighted as key to maintaining market share gains.

Grocery and pharmacy expansion: Amazon saw rapid growth in fresh groceries, Everyday Essentials, and pharmacy services. Olsavsky stated that Prime members ordering groceries with same-day delivery have tripled year-over-year, and pharmacy users increased over 60% year-over-year, supporting cross-category spend and customer retention.

Advertising platform transition: The advertising segment experienced slower growth due to timing shifts of Prime Day and changes in search engine marketing. However, management expects growth to return to the high teens, supported by the rollout of the Amazon Ads Agent, which integrates AI-driven campaign management and optimization tools.

Profitability has become increasingly concentrated among companies controlling the infrastructure, software, and platforms supporting the digital economy, and investors are increasingly looking towards the most profitable stocks of the past five years to make sense of the ongoing market trends. Artificial intelligence has accelerated this trend, creating enormous demand for advanced semiconductors, memory chips, and cloud computing capacity. Meanwhile, digital advertising, enterprise software, consumer technology, and financial services continue to generate substantial earnings through established customer relationships and recurring revenue.

The semiconductor industry has emerged as a particularly significant beneficiary. Companies such as NVIDIA, Micron, and SK hynix are capitalizing on demand for AI computing and memory, while Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company profits from manufacturing the advanced chips used across the industry. However, these businesses are exposed to different risks. Memory manufacturers depend heavily on supply and pricing conditions, while chip designers must sustain demand for increasingly expensive computing systems. Cloud computing presents a different financial equation. Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet are generating substantial revenue from businesses purchasing digital infrastructure, but expanding their computing capacity requires enormous investment. According to Reuters, second-quarter S&P 500 earnings were on track to increase 52% year over year in 2026, supported by a 74% profit jump in the technology ‌sector. This is compared with 33% when substantial investment-related gains were excluded, according to Tajinder Dhillon, head of earnings research at LSEG. A company can continue increasing profits while delivering disappointing shareholder returns if its valuation already assumes even faster growth. Amazon (AMZN) disclosed an $80 billion secured loan facility that pledges data center equipment as collateral, departing from its usual cash and bond funding.

Amazon's total contractual commitments hit $884 billion at September 30, more than doubling year-over-year, with $160 billion locked in for property and equipment.

Recently, Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) disclosed a secured loan facility of up to approximately $80.0 billion in its third-quarter 10-Q, filed October 30, 2026. Amazon has mostly paid for its expansion with cash and plain corporate bonds, so offering the equipment itself as security is a new step.

David Ryder / Getty Images

The shares fell 1.41% to $240.35 on October 30 and traded at $240.83 after hours at 7:54 p.m. ET. Tech stocks sold off broadly that day, so the drop can't be attributed to the facility.

AMZN Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.

AWS demand looks strong enough to justify the spending. But the cash bill is now bigger than what the business brings in, and Amazon is using financing tools it used to leave to rivals.

What Amazon's $80 Billion Facility Actually Covers

The facility allows "borrowings at our discretion, from Q1 2027 through Q3 2028," at variable interest rates, according to the filing. Amazon has set up the ability to borrow, but it hasn't drawn anything yet and can't until 2027.

Each borrowing comes due five years after it is drawn. Amazon "will grant a security interest in certain purchased assets," which means lenders get a claim on some of the equipment if Amazon doesn't repay.
